newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Arctic could set first for gender equality.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Arctic could set first for gender equality.

text.p: Depending on the outcome of a vote on Monday, Canada's thinly populated eastern Arctic could become the first place in the world where the legislature is required to seat an equal number of men and women.

Residents of the remote region -- which will become a separate territory under Canada called Nunavut in 1999 -- were voting in a plebiscite on the shape of their future government. The vast eastern Arctic, which spans three time zones and extends to the North Pole, is home to a mere 25,000 people, many of them Inuit or Eskimo.

The idea, first raised two years ago by the commission overseeing the creation of the new territory, has proven controversial. Results of the voting were expected to be known late on Monday or early on Tuesday.

Ironically, some of the most outspoken critics of the idea have been women. Some female leaders contended the measure would amount to a quota system that suggests they could not defeat male candidates on their own merits.

If voters approve the so-called "gender parity" proposal, residents will cast two ballots in an upcoming election to form Nunavut's first legislative assembly -- one from a list of male candidates and one from a list of female candidates.

"I think in today's system there's a lack of communication between the two sexes. There's lack of understanding and, in many instances, a lack of respect," said chief commissioner John Amagoalik and a supporter of the proposal.
"I think this will result in a wider view when things are considered at the Nunavut legislative assembly."
The plan is aimed at ensuring balanced representation of men and women in the legislature. The overall response has been mixed but some political analysts believe it will win.

Women make up just over half of Nunavut's population, but their numbers are dramatically under-represented in the current legislative assembly for the Northwest Territories in Yellowknife. Just two of 24 seats there, or 8 percent, are held by women. Nunavut is being formed by splitting the Northwest Territories.

But one of the proposal's most vocal opponents is the Northwest Territories' Minister Responsible for the Status of Women, Manitok Thompson, who said the new system would restrict her political freedom.
"I don't believe that it is right to put me as a woman in a position where for the rest of my political career, I will only be able to run against women," Thompson said.

In some conservative religious communities, Inuit men and women alike have protested publicly that gender parity contravenes the teachings of the Bible. At some meetings on the proposal, wives have defied their husbands, openly supporting the principle of equality of the sexes.

"I have a mind, I have dreams, I can accomplish just as much as a man. There's nothing I cannot accomplish that a man can accomplish," one Inuit woman in the tiny outpost of Pangnirtung said during a recent gathering.
Rita Arey, president of the Northwest Territories Status of Women Council, said a gender-equal legislature would fit with traditional Inuit culture.
"Women's opinions were respected and sought out because they provided balance and harmony in decisions affecting the well-being of the community as a whole. We must regain this balance."
